Elara was a wisp of a girl, all sharp angles and hollows, carved by a life of scarcity. In her small, drafty home where a full belly was a rare and celebrated event, she harbored a secret, desperate dream. While other girls wished for ribbons or pretty dolls, Elara wished for fat. To her, fat was beautiful. It was a sign of security, of never having to hear her own stomach groan in the silent night. It was a soft armor against the sharp edges of the world.

She saw them sometimes in town, the wives of merchants, their arms soft and dimpled, their chins doubling in contentment. They were not invisible. They took up space. They were solid, present, and undeniable. Elara, in her thinness, felt like a ghost, easily overlooked and forgotten.

One day, clutching her resolve, she walked into "The Golden Ladle," a restaurant known less for its cuisine and more for its convenient location. The owner, a perpetually weary man named Mr. Gable, was about to shoo her away when she made her proposition.

"I'll work as your waitress," she said, her voice thin but steady. "I'll clean, I'll serve, I'll do anything. You don't have to pay me a single coin."

Mr. Gable narrowed his eyes, suspicious. "What's the catch?"

"A place to sleep," Elara said, gesturing to a small, dusty storage room in the back. "And the leftovers. Whatever the customers don't eat, I get to."

He laughed, a short, harsh bark. The food at The Golden Ladle was legendarily bad. The stews were watery, the meat was tough, and the bread was always a day past its prime. More than half of every plate came back to the kitchen. "You want our garbage?" he sneered.

"One man's garbage," Elara replied with a strange light in her eyes, "is another woman's feast."

The deal was struck. Mr. Gable congratulated himself on his cleverness, having secured a free, tireless worker. Elara, for the first time in her life, felt a thrill of hope.

Her first night was a revelation. Mountains of half-eaten, greasy potatoes, congealed sauces, rejected cutlets, and soggy vegetables were piled onto a platter for her. To anyone else, it would have been nauseating. To Elara, it was paradise. She ate until her stomach, unaccustomed to such volume, ached in protest. But it was a good ache. An ache of fullness.

The weeks turned into months. Elara was a diligent worker, but her true labor began after the last customer left. Night after night, she devoured the remnants of Mr. Gable's culinary failures. The transformation began subtly. The hollows in her cheeks began to fill. Her collarbones became less pronounced. She felt a new, pleasing weight to her limbs. Each pound she gained was a victory, a brick in the fortress she was building around herself.

Mr. Gable had to let out the seams of her uniform, then order a larger one, and then a larger one still. Customers started to notice the change. The whisper-thin girl who used to flit between tables now moved with a deliberate, heavy tread. Her body, once a fragile frame, was becoming a vast, soft landscape.

Her goal, once a distant dream, became an all-consuming reality. She ate with a singular focus, her world shrinking to the plate in front of her. She was no longer just eating to be full; she was eating to become.

Then came the day it happened. She had grown so immense that her antechamber, once ample, was now a snug fit. Needing to use the staff's small water closet, she wedged herself into the hallway. But the doorway to the WC was narrower. She pushed, feeling the frame dig into her soft flesh, and became stuck. Panic, cold and sharp, pierced through her euphoric haze. She was trapped. After a great, painful struggle, with Mr. Gable pushing from the other side, she was dislodged, but the truth was undeniable: she no longer fit.

From that day on, her world became the kitchen, the main dining room, and her storeroom bed. The bathroom was inaccessible. The front door was an impossible dream. She was a prisoner of her own success.

A grim new reality set in. With no access to sanitation, her small living space began to sour. A cloying, unpleasant odor started to seep out of her room, clinging to the curtains and tablecloths of the dining room. Elara, trapped in her massive body, had no choice but to live in her own accumulating filth.

Customers began to complain. They would wrinkle their noses upon entering, their appetites vanishing before they even saw a menu. "What is that smell?" they'd mutter, quickly leaving. Business at The Golden Ladle, already poor, plummeted.

Mr. Gable was in despair. His free waitress had become a monstrous, immovable symbol of his restaurant's decay. He raged at her, but it was useless. She couldn't leave. He couldn't force her out. The smell grew worse, a thick, unavoidable presence that drove away even the least discerning of diners.

Finally, the day came when no one came at all. The bills piled up, and Mr. Gable, broken and bankrupt, simply gave up. He packed a small bag, locked the cash register (which was empty anyway), and walked to the front door. He paused and looked back at the colossal figure of Elara, who sat on her reinforced bed in the dim light, a monument to a misguided dream. He didn't say a word. He just opened the door and walked out, not looking back.

The lock clicked shut, echoing in the cavernous silence.

Elara was alone. The restaurant was dark, the chairs were overturned, and a thick layer of dust was already settling on the tables. The source of her glorious transformation—the endless supply of food—was gone. All that remained was the silence, the filth, and her own monumental body. She had wanted to take up space, to be solid and undeniable. And she had succeeded. She was a mountain of a woman, a permanent fixture in an abandoned restaurant, left alone with the crushing, absolute weight of her wish come true.
